interactions.summary: Jiang briefly consolidates the seminar's working contrasts between love and lust before moving into the next canto.
A participant reads Canto 6 and early Canto 7: Cerberus, Ciacco, Florentine schism, envy-pride-avarice, and Virgil's answer about punishment after the Last Judgment.
Jiang interprets Virgil's handling of Cerberus as another sign that he rules hell's lower powers with imperial authority.

speaker_notes.note: The long reading spans multiple canto transitions and blends quoted narration with dialogue from the poem, but it is still clearly student reading rather than Jiang exposition.

claims.claim: Jiang summarizes the room's provisional distinction by saying love gives itself to a person's full complexity while lust objectifies, possesses, and seeks control.
Jiang reads Virgil's feeding of Cerberus as evidence that Virgil functions like an emperor of hell who can command or pacify demons.
claims.temporal_scope: Interpretive claim made in the seminar on 2026-06-21.

claims.claim: The quoted Ciacco passage treats Florence as a city consumed by envy, pride, and avarice, with factional bloodshed and very few just men.
claims.temporal_scope: Poetic evidence read in the seminar on 2026-06-21.

claims.claim: The reading presents a scholastic rule for hell after the final judgment: greater perfection brings greater capacity for pleasure or pain, so the damned will feel punishment more fully.
claims.temporal_scope: Poetic doctrine read in the seminar on 2026-06-21.

signature_moments.moment: Virgil does not merely guide through hell; Jiang says he feeds Cerberus and thereby looks like hell's own emperor.
signature_moments.source_phrase: virgil really is the emperor of hell
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This pushes the seminar's emerging suspicion that Virgil is not a neutral escort but a figure deeply at home in the infernal order.

signature_moments.moment: Ciacco compresses Florence's disease into three sparks that set every heart on fire: envy, pride, and avarice.
signature_moments.source_phrase: three Sparks that set on fire every heart are envy pride and avariciousness
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It is a strong reusable formula for Dante's political anthropology.

signature_moments.moment: Punishment intensifies after resurrection because fuller being means fuller suffering as well as fuller pleasure.
signature_moments.source_phrase: when a thing has more perfection so much the greater is its pain or pleasure
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This gives the infernal economy an unsettling metaphysical logic rather than a purely physical one.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The glutton in Florence whose speech links personal vice to civic faction and prophecy.
Dante's compact triad for Florence's political corruption: envy, pride, and avarice.

chronology_notes.note: This June 21, 2026 packet marks the seminar's transition from the erotic problem of Francesca into hell's civic and metaphysical architecture: demon authority, Florentine schism, and post-judgment punishment.

uncertainty_notes.note: Several names and lines in the reading are ASR-degraded, but Cerberus, Ciacco, the Florentine faction passage, and the perfection/punishment doctrine remain identifiable.
